division.heading: Lawyers’ Charges, Retainer Agreements and Right of Review

operative_text.controlling:
10.3(1)  A lawyer may charge lawyer’s fees for services performed
as a lawyer whether or not the lawyer is also acting in the capacity
of a guardian, mortgagee, personal representative or trustee.
(2)  Despite subrule (1), a lawyer acting as a guardian, mortgagee,
personal representative or trustee is not entitled to be paid out of or
to charge to a trust, an estate, a fund, mortgaged property or a
mortgage loan for which the lawyer performs lawyer’s services
unless
(a) the Court orders the amount paid or charged,
(b) every person interested in the trust, estate, fund,
mortgaged property or mortgage loan is legally competent
and agrees to the payment or the charge, or
(c) the lawyer’s charges have been reviewed and certified by
a review officer.
(3)  This rule does not apply to client funds held by a lawyer in the
lawyer’s trust account.

BOOK_A.title: Lawyer Acting in Representative Capacity
BOOK_A.commentary:
trustee
A lawyer can act both as executor and as the lawyer for the estate, and bill for that; but if he
or she does, the roles have to be kept distinct, and careful records made to distinguish the two.³
A lawyer cannot justify a bill to an estate on the grounds that the deceased had agreed to the
method of billing, without corroboration of the lawyer’s evidence about the agreement, particularly
where on its face the agreement alleged seems to produce too high a fee.⁴
On an agreement about fees to an estate, see the Salmon case.⁵
If a co-trustee and guardian of an estate is a solicitor, the court must approve his or her fees
or disbursements, and if they are taken without approval, the court can review the charges and
order some paid back.⁶
If the solicitor does clerical work for the estate, the charges for that should
be lower than lawyers’ rates.⁷
